_help: Facts she shares when you say yes. Fact_Elite = game lore, Fact_Real = real space, Fact_Planets = planet and star types. One fact per line, a couple of sentences.
Fact_Elite: Elite Dangerous was released on the 16th of December 2014, thirty years after the very first Elite appeared in 1984.
The original Elite was written by two Cambridge students, David Braben and Ian Bell.
The first Elite fitted eight whole galaxies into a tiny amount of memory by generating the stars from a formula instead of storing them.
The original Elite used simple wireframe 3D graphics, and it was one of the first games where you could roam an open universe and choose your own career.
Frontier Developments, the studio behind Elite Dangerous, was founded by David Braben in 1994.
Elite Dangerous was crowdfunded. Its Kickstarter began on the 5th of November 2012, and 25,681 backers pledged about one and a half million pounds.
The Kickstarter for Elite Dangerous reached its goal 48 hours before the deadline.
The galaxy in Elite Dangerous is a one to one scale model of the Milky Way, with around 400 billion star systems.
About 150,000 of the star systems in Elite Dangerous come from real astronomical catalogues, including Sol and Alpha Centauri.
The star systems that aren't from real catalogues are generated by a program called the Stellar Forge, using models based on real science.
The galaxy map of Elite Dangerous is divided into 42 named galactic regions.
There are 141 nebulae in Elite Dangerous, each based on a real nebula in the Milky Way.
If you look out of your cockpit in Elite Dangerous, you can see 32 other galaxies in the distance.
The in-game year runs in step with real time, and it is always our year plus 1286.
Elite Dangerous is set in the 34th century, and it began in the year 3300.
The three great powers of Elite Dangerous are the Federation, the Empire and the Alliance of Independent Systems.
The Empire's capital is Achenar, and the Alliance's capital is Alioth.
Powerplay arrived in June 2015, letting commanders pledge to powers and fight over the control of systems.
The Horizons expansion arrived on the 15th of December 2015 and let commanders land on planets and drive an SRV.
The Odyssey expansion arrived in May 2021 and let commanders walk around on foot for the first time.
In November 2025, Elite Dangerous let players begin building up and colonising new systems for themselves.
The Guardians are an extinct alien civilisation, and their ruins were first found by players in October 2016.
The first Guardian ruins were found by a commander called XDeath, in a system named Synuefe XR-H d11-102.
The Thargoids got their name from blurry footage in the year 2849, which showed an alien ship with the letters T H A R G on its hull.
The first Thargoid war lasted from 3125 until 3151.
Thargoids can pull ships out of hyperspace in an event called a hyperdiction.
Thargoid barnacles are tall structures that extract resources from planets, and they are often a warning sign of something bigger.
Thargoid Titans are vast ships, and there were eight of them, hidden in hive structures called Maelstroms.
Thargoid Interceptors carry a Thargoid heart, which repairs their hull while they fight.
The Thargoid Scouts have no heart, which makes them far easier to damage than an Interceptor.
Sagittarius A star, the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, is a real place you can fly to in Elite Dangerous.
Beagle Point is about 65,279 light years from Sol, and it is one of the most famous destinations in the game.
Beagle Point was named after the ship DSS Beagle, which was itself named after the beloved pet beagle of explorer Kamzel.
Colonia is around 22,000 light years from Sol. For a while it was the most remote inhabited system in the game.
The Colonia Connection Highway is a chain of 17 inhabited systems with 20 ports, linking the Core Systems to Colonia.
Jaques Station, a huge station able to make star jumps, was stranded in the system now called Colonia after a failed jump in May 3302.
Jaques Station was found by pilots on the 29th of June 3302, and an aid convoy brought it partly back to life.
The Distant Worlds expedition of 3302 sent more than a thousand commanders on a journey to Beagle Point.
Hutton Orbital is an outpost in the Alpha Centauri system, and it is so far from the arrival star that its light would take about 78 days to reach you.
Hutton Orbital is more than six million light seconds from the arrival star, and it is famous among players for being a very long trip.
The Hutton Mug is a rare item that won a community vote, and it is sold only at Hutton Orbital.
Raxxla is a legendary location that no commander has ever publicly been able to find, and it is one of the longest running mysteries in Elite.
Raxxla was first mentioned in The Dark Wheel, the novella that came packed with the original Elite in 1984.
The original Elite began in a system called Lave, which still exists in Elite Dangerous today.
The Cobra Mark Three, one of the most famous ships in Elite Dangerous, was already the star of the original Elite in 1984.
The Coriolis station, with its famous mail slot entrance, first appeared in the original Elite.
The ships Sidewinder, Viper, Python and Mamba all appeared in the 1984 Elite, and they are still in the game today.
The Anaconda, the Python and the Cobra Mark Three are all built by Faulcon DeLacy.
The Imperial Cutter is built by Gutamaya, and it is one of the largest ships a commander can fly.
The Type Nine Heavy and the Asp Explorer are both built by Lakon Spaceways.
The Sidewinder, the Adder and the Fer-de-Lance are all made by Zorgon Peterson.
The Federal Corvette is built by Core Dynamics, the same company that makes the Eagle.
The Dolphin, the Orca and the Beluga Liner are all built by Saud Kruger, a maker of passenger ships.
There are more than forty different ships you can fly in Elite Dangerous.
Supercruise in Elite Dangerous lets you travel at many times the speed of light, and at the top end it can exceed two thousand times light speed.
You can only scoop fuel from stars of the classes K, G, B, F, O, A and M, which spells K G B F O A M, or KGB Foam.
Flying close to a neutron star's jet cone supercharges your frame shift drive, and it can quadruple your next jump range.
White dwarf stars can supercharge your drive too, but only by about fifty percent.
Staying too long in a neutron star's jet cone can damage the modules of your ship, and even tear it apart.
FSD injections made from materials can boost your jump range by 25, 50 or 100 percent, depending on the grade.
Fleet carriers are player owned, and they can travel up to 500 light years in a single jump.
Every tonne of cargo you carry lowers your jump range, which is why explorers fly stripped down.
The frame shift drive cannot charge while you are mass locked by something big nearby, like a station, a planet or another ship.
A docking computer can dock your ship for you at a station, and while it works it plays The Blue Danube waltz.
Silent running lets you reduce your heat signature, which helps you hide from ships scanning for you.
The SRV that comes with Horizons is called the Scarab, and it can drive on any landable world.
The Maverick, Artemis and Dominator are the three kinds of suits that commanders wear in Odyssey.
Each biological species in Odyssey needs three samples, which the game calls log, sample and analyse.
You have to walk a minimum distance between samples of the same species, so you can't just scan the same plant three times.
Odyssey's biological life is found on many worlds with an atmosphere, even a very thin one.
Galnet is the in-game news service, and its stories often reflect what the real players have done in the game.
Community goals let thousands of commanders work towards one shared target, and Galnet reports on how it went.
In Elite Dangerous, you can choose to play in Open, in Solo, or in a private group of friends.
Elite Dangerous runs on Frontier's own engine, called Cobra.
The music of Elite Dangerous: Odyssey was composed by Dan Millidge.
The engineer Felicity Farseer specialises in making your frame shift drive better, and many explorers visit her.
The Pilots Federation is the organisation that gives every commander their rank, from Harmless all the way up to Elite.
In the Elite Dangerous galaxy, the Core Systems around Sol are the most heavily populated and the best connected.
The Abyss is a sparsely populated area of the northern Milky Way between two spiral arms, and Beagle Point sits within it.
Colonia lies in the Inner Scutum-Centaurus Arm of the galaxy.
The Thargoids' second war with humanity involved ships called Interceptors attacking stations in the Core Systems.
A Thargoid surface site is a huge structure on a planet, guarded by scavengers and full of Thargoid eggs and unknown devices.
Thargoid barnacles are known to produce a strange material called meta-alloy.
Fact_Real: The Milky Way is roughly 100,000 light years across, and it holds somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars.
Our Sun sits about 26,000 light years from the centre of the Milky Way, in a quiet stretch between two spiral arms.
The Sun takes roughly 230 million years to complete one orbit around the centre of the galaxy.
At the centre of the Milky Way is a black hole called Sagittarius A star, about four million times the mass of the Sun.
In 2022, astronomers released the first image of Sagittarius A star, our own galaxy's black hole.
The first ever picture of a black hole was released in April 2019, showing the giant black hole in the galaxy Messier 87.
The Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million light years away, and it is heading towards the Milky Way.
The Milky Way and Andromeda are expected to merge in around four to five billion years.
The observable universe is about 93 billion light years across, even though it is only 13.8 billion years old.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year, which is nearly 9.5 trillion kilometres.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach the Earth.
The nearest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light years away.
Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky, is only about 8.6 light years from Earth.
When you look at the stars, you are looking back in time, because their light left them years or even millennia ago.
There are probably more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches.
Most of the stars in the Milky Way are red dwarfs, smaller and cooler than the Sun.
Red dwarf stars burn their fuel so slowly that they can shine for trillions of years.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old, and it is roughly halfway through its life.
The Sun makes up about 99.86 percent of all the mass in our solar system.
In around five billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant, and later shrink into a white dwarf.
The Sun is a G-type star, and astronomers class it as a G2V.
Stars are classified by temperature using the letters O, B, A, F, G, K and M, with O the hottest and M the coolest.
The hottest stars, the O class, burn blue-white and can be over 30,000 degrees at the surface.
A white dwarf is the leftover core of a star like the Sun, packing roughly the mass of the Sun into something Earth-sized.
A teaspoon of white dwarf material would weigh several tonnes.
A neutron star is only about 20 kilometres across, yet it can have more mass than our Sun.
A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh billions of tonnes.
Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space like lighthouses.
The first pulsar was discovered in 1967 by a young astronomer called Jocelyn Bell Burnell.
The fastest known pulsar spins about 716 times every second.
Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields known in the universe.
The Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun, is the heaviest a white dwarf can be before it collapses further.
A brown dwarf is a failed star, too small to fuse ordinary hydrogen, but bigger than a giant planet.
Wolf-Rayet stars are massive, extremely hot stars that blow off their outer layers in powerful stellar winds.
T Tauri stars are very young stars that haven't yet settled into steady hydrogen fusion.
Supernovae can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.
Supernova 1987A, in a neighbouring galaxy called the Large Magellanic Cloud, was the closest supernova seen in centuries.
The last supernova in our own galaxy that people saw with the naked eye was in 1604, and it is called Kepler's supernova.
In the year 1054, astronomers in China recorded a bright new star, and its remains are now the Crab Nebula.
The red supergiant Betelgeuse will explode as a supernova some day, probably within about a hundred thousand years.
Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners. If the Sun were swapped for a black hole of the same mass, the planets would keep orbiting normally.
Gravity slows down time, an effect measured with atomic clocks on Earth, and near a black hole it becomes extreme.
The edge of a black hole, beyond which nothing can escape, is called the event horizon.
Stephen Hawking predicted that black holes slowly leak radiation, which is now called Hawking radiation.
Gravitational waves, ripples in space and time, were first detected directly in September 2015.
The Orion Nebula is a huge stellar nursery, and you can see it with the naked eye as the fuzzy middle star of Orion's sword.
The Pillars of Creation, in the Eagle Nebula, are towers of gas and dust several light years tall, where new stars are forming.
The Helix Nebula, sometimes called the Eye of God, is the dying remains of a Sun-like star only around 650 light years away.
The Horsehead Nebula is a dark cloud of dust silhouetted against glowing gas in the constellation Orion.
The Crab Nebula has a pulsar at its heart, spinning about thirty times a second.
Nebulae are the nurseries and graveyards of stars, glowing clouds of gas and dust.
The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are two small galaxies that orbit the Milky Way, and they are visible from the southern hemisphere.
Gamma ray bursts are the most energetic explosions known, and one can release in seconds as much energy as the Sun will in its whole lifetime.
A fast radio burst is a flash of radio waves from deep space that lasts only a few milliseconds.
Most of the matter in the universe is dark matter, which we cannot see but whose gravity we can measure.
Everything we can see, stars, planets and galaxies, makes up only about five percent of the universe's energy and matter.
Some galaxies, called quasars, have central black holes feeding so fiercely that they outshine all the stars in the galaxy.
The Voyager 1 probe, launched in 1977, left the Sun's bubble and entered interstellar space in 2012.
Voyager 1 is now almost a full light day away from Earth, and it is still sending back data.
Voyager 1 and 2 each carry a golden record containing sounds and images from Earth.
A famous photograph taken by Voyager 1 in 1990 showed Earth as a tiny speck, and Carl Sagan called it the Pale Blue Dot.
The Oort Cloud is a vast shell of icy bodies that may stretch a light year or more from the Sun.
The Kuiper Belt is a ring of icy worlds beyond Neptune, home to Pluto.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and New Horizons flew past it in July 2015.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, and it orbits above the Earth's atmosphere.
The James Webb Space Telescope has a 6.5 metre mirror made of 18 gold-coated hexagonal segments.
The James Webb Space Telescope sits about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, and it observes the universe mainly in infrared.
There are more than six thousand confirmed planets orbiting other stars.
The first planet found around a Sun-like star was 51 Pegasi b, discovered in 1995, and its discoverers won a Nobel Prize in 2019.
The very first exoplanets ever confirmed were found in 1992, orbiting a pulsar.
TRAPPIST-1 is a small star about 40 light years away with seven Earth-sized planets orbiting it.
Proxima Centauri has a planet in its habitable zone, called Proxima b, only 4.24 light years from us.
Kepler-16b was the first confirmed planet orbiting two stars at once, like Tatooine from Star Wars.
Rogue planets drift through the galaxy without orbiting any star at all.
Light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Earth to the Moon.
Space is silent, because there is no air to carry sound.
Astronauts get slightly taller in space, because their spines stretch without gravity pressing down.
The International Space Station travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour, and it orbits the Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
Astronauts on the International Space Station see about 16 sunrises and sunsets every day.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on the 12th of April 1961.
Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, was launched on the 4th of October 1957.
The Apollo 11 astronauts landed on the Moon in July 1969.
The Moon is slowly drifting away from the Earth at about 3.8 centimetres a year.
There is a thin cloud of space dust and gas between the stars called the interstellar medium.
The cosmic microwave background is the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, and it fills the whole sky.
The universe is expanding, and the farthest galaxies are moving away from us faster than light because space itself is stretching.
At very nearly the speed of light, crossing the Milky Way would take about 100,000 years for people watching, but only a short time for the traveller.
The Sun loses about four million tonnes of mass every second, as it turns matter into energy.
A day on Venus is longer than its year.
The light leaving the Sun's surface spent tens of thousands of years working its way out from the core, yet it takes just eight minutes to reach us.
Fact_Planets: Earth-like worlds are among the rarest and most valuable finds in the galaxy, with liquid water and an atmosphere that makes them look just like home from orbit.
A water world is covered by a deep global ocean, and in reality scientists think such ocean worlds could be common.
An ammonia world has an atmosphere and surface chemistry built around ammonia, which could in theory support exotic forms of life.
A terraformable planet is a world that could, with enough technology, be reshaped into something much more like Earth.
A high metal content world is a rocky world with a larger share of metal in its makeup than a plain rocky one.
A metal-rich body is made of rock with an unusually large amount of metals in it, which makes it denser than an ordinary rocky world.
A rocky ice body is a world made of a mix of rock and frozen water and gases, found in the colder outer parts of a system.
An icy body is made mostly of frozen water, ammonia and methane, like many moons in our own outer solar system.
Gas giants are classed from one to five by temperature, using a scheme proposed by the astronomer David Sudarsky.
A Class One gas giant is cold, and its pale blue-white clouds are made of ammonia, like Jupiter and Saturn.
A Class Two gas giant is a little warmer, and its bright white clouds are made of water vapour.
A Class Three gas giant is hot enough to have no clouds, so it looks like a deep blue ball of clear gas.
A Class Four gas giant is scorching, with clouds of alkali metals like sodium and potassium.
A Class Five gas giant is a so-called hot Jupiter, so hot that its clouds are made of silicates, which are droplets of melted rock and sand.
A water giant is a huge world with a great deal of water in its makeup, a bit like our own ice giants, Uranus and Neptune.
A helium-rich gas giant has a much higher share of helium than the gas giants we know, which is an unusual twist on the usual hydrogen mix.
Gas giants with life are extremely rare in Elite Dangerous, and finding one is a special moment for any explorer.
Hot Jupiters are gas giants that orbit extremely close to their stars, with years that last only a few days.
On the hot Jupiter HD 189733 b, scientists think it might rain molten glass sideways in winds faster than the speed of sound.
On the hot planet WASP-76 b, astronomers have found hints of iron vapour that may condense into rain on the cooler night side.
The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface. It is often called the Goldilocks zone.
Tidally locked planets always show the same face to their star, like the Moon does to the Earth.
On a tidally locked world, one side bakes in permanent daylight while the other freezes in endless night, with a twilight ring between them.
The Roche limit is the distance within which a moon gets torn apart by its planet's gravity, and it is why planetary rings can exist.
Planetary rings are made of countless pieces of ice and rock, from dust specks to chunks the size of buildings.
Saturn's rings are mostly water ice, and they are huge in width but incredibly thin, in places only about ten metres thick.
Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a big enough bathtub of water.
Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets in our solar system put together.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm that has been raging for at least centuries, and it is wider than the Earth.
Neptune has the fastest winds of any planet in our solar system, reaching over two thousand kilometres an hour.
Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, tilted at about 98 degrees, probably after an ancient collision.
Scientists think it might rain diamonds deep inside Uranus and Neptune, where extreme pressure squeezes carbon.
Venus is the hottest planet in our solar system, at around 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead.
Venus spins backwards compared to most planets, so the Sun rises in the west there.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, yet it has water ice in permanently shadowed craters near its poles.
A year on Mercury lasts only 88 Earth days.
Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.
Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos, shaped like lumpy potatoes.
The Valles Marineris on Mars is a canyon system roughly as long as the United States is wide.
Phobos is slowly spiralling towards Mars, and in tens of millions of years it will break up into a ring.
Titan, a moon of Saturn, has lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane, and a thick orange atmosphere.
The Huygens probe landed on Titan in January 2005, the farthest landing ever made from Earth.
Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, shoots geysers of water into space from an ocean hidden beneath its ice.
Europa, a moon of Jupiter, hides a global ocean beneath its icy shell, with more water than all of Earth's oceans.
Io, a moon of Jupiter, is the most volcanically active body in our solar system.
Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is the largest moon in the solar system, even bigger than the planet Mercury.
Triton, the largest moon of Neptune, orbits backwards, which suggests it was captured from the Kuiper Belt.
Our Moon is probably the result of a Mars-sized body crashing into the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
Pluto has a huge heart-shaped region of nitrogen ice, called Tombaugh Regio.
A planet is called a super-Earth if it is larger than Earth but smaller than Neptune, even though it may not be Earth-like at all.
A planet in the habitable zone isn't automatically habitable, because it also needs the right atmosphere and the right mass.
Planets with thin atmospheres can still feel pleasant for a surface explorer, but a thin atmosphere offers little protection from radiation.
Landing on a high gravity world is dangerous, because a ship that is already heavy has to work much harder to take off.
Gravity on a planet depends on both its mass and its radius, so a bigger world isn't always a heavier pull on your feet.
A planet's atmosphere is held in place by its gravity, which is why small worlds like Mercury and our Moon have almost none.
Magnetic fields help shield a planet's atmosphere from the solar wind, and Earth's comes from molten iron churning in its core.
Mars lost most of its atmosphere over billions of years, probably helped along by the loss of its global magnetic field.
Volcanic worlds can have lava lakes and sulphur plains, like Io, where volcanic plumes rise hundreds of kilometres.
Atmospheric pressure on Venus's surface is about 90 times that of Earth, similar to being nearly a kilometre under the sea.
A planet's colour can tell you a lot. Blue often means water or methane, red often means iron oxide, and white often means ice or clouds.
A planet in the habitable zone might still be dead, which is why scientists also study the gases in its atmosphere.
Oxygen and methane together in an atmosphere are a strong hint of life, because both would normally destroy each other without something replenishing them.
Most known exoplanets were found by watching stars dim slightly as a planet passes in front, which is called the transit method.
Astronomers can also find planets by the tiny wobble they cause in their star, called the radial velocity method.
Some planets orbit so close to their stars that the surface is molten rock, and astronomers call them lava worlds.
Gas dwarfs, also called mini-Neptunes, are planets larger than Earth, but smaller than Neptune, with thick hydrogen atmospheres.
Moons of moons, sometimes called submoons, are possible in theory, but tides usually tear them away.
A planet's day is just how long it takes to spin once, and it can be much longer or shorter than its year.
In Elite Dangerous, landable planets are the ones with surfaces you can touch down on, but gas giants have no surface to land on at all.
Many of the most beautiful planets in Elite Dangerous have rings, because ring systems are natural around large worlds.
Planets can orbit a pair of stars at once, in what astronomers call circumbinary orbits.
The planets in our solar system all orbit in nearly the same plane, which tells us they formed from a flat spinning disc of gas and dust.
Rocky worlds form close to a star, where ice is boiled away, and gas giants form farther out, beyond the frost line, where ice survives.
Tiny dust grains stick together to form pebbles, then boulders, then planetesimals, and finally planets, in a process called accretion.
The Earth's core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Earth is the only place in the universe we know of that has life, but astronomers think the ingredients for it are common.
